Backward recursion avoids having to enumerate states
The terminal cost is unknown until the first step is taken
check.why: J_k is defined in terms of J_k+1, so you need the future optimal costs first, starting from the known terminal cost. DP still enumerates states, which is the curse of dimensionality.

dynamic_programming.tryIt: On a 5-node directed graph with edge costs, compute shortest costs-to-go to a goal by backward DP by hand, then read off the optimal next node from every node.

points: Value iteration repeats V_k+1(s) = max_a [R(s, a) + γ Σ P(s'|s,a) V_k(s')]; the Bellman operator is a γ-contraction, so V_k converges to V* from any start.
Policy iteration alternates evaluation (solve V_π = R_π + γ P_π V_π exactly) and improvement (π(s) = argmax_a of the one-step lookahead), and terminates in finitely many iterations.
Both need the full model P and R; policy iteration usually needs few iterations but each is expensive, while value iteration has cheap iterations but may need many as γ approaches 1.

check.q: You raise the discount factor γ from 0.9 to 0.99 in value iteration. What happens to convergence?
choices: It speeds up, since future rewards are weighted more strongly
It is unchanged, since convergence depends only on the state count
It slows down, since error shrinks by a factor γ per iteration
It stops converging, since the Bellman operator is no longer a contraction
check.why: The error bound shrinks by γ per sweep, so γ = 0.99 needs roughly 10 times more iterations than 0.9. It is still a contraction for any γ < 1.

value_policy_iteration.tryIt: Implement value iteration on a 4x4 gridworld with a +1 goal and -0.04 step cost; count iterations to reach max change below 1e-6 for γ = 0.9 and γ = 0.99.

points: In RL the agent does not know P or R; it interacts with the environment, observing (s, a, r, s') tuples, and must learn a good policy from this experience.
Exploration versus exploitation: acting greedily on current estimates can miss better actions, so strategies like ε-greedy or optimism deliberately try uncertain actions.
Methods split into model-free (learn values or policies directly) and model-based (learn dynamics, then plan), and into on-policy versus off-policy depending on which policy generated the data.

check.q: An agent always takes the action with the highest current value estimate from the start, with values initialized to zero. What is the main risk?
choices: Its value estimates will diverge to infinity
It will need a model of the transition probabilities
It will explore too much and never exploit
It may lock onto an early action and never find better ones
check.why: Pure greedy behavior never tests actions that look worse, so an early lucky outcome can trap it in a suboptimal choice. Divergence is a different issue, related to function approximation and off-policy bootstrapping.

rl_fundamentals.tryIt: Simulate a 10-armed bandit with Gaussian rewards and compare average reward over 1000 steps for ε = 0, 0.01, and 0.1 using sample-average value estimates.

points: Monte Carlo estimates V(s) by averaging complete returns G_t observed after visiting s; it is unbiased but has high variance and must wait until episode end.
TD(0) updates V(s) toward r + γ V(s') after each step: V(s) += α [r + γ V(s') - V(s)], bootstrapping from the current estimate of the next state.
TD learns online and has lower variance but is biased by its own estimates; n-step returns and TD(λ) interpolate between TD(0) and Monte Carlo.

check.q: A task has very long episodes and noisy rewards, and you need to update values during an episode. Which choice fits best and why?
choices: Monte Carlo, because it is unbiased and the bias of TD would dominate
TD learning, because it updates every step and reduces variance
Monte Carlo, because it works without knowing the reward function
TD learning, because it requires no discount factor at all
check.why: TD updates online after each transition and its bootstrapped target has lower variance than full noisy returns. Monte Carlo must wait for episode end; both are model-free, so that is not a distinguishing factor.

td_learning.tryIt: On the 5-state random walk (terminal reward 1 on the right), run MC and TD(0) for 100 episodes with α = 0.1 and compare RMS error against the true values 1/6, 2/6, ..., 5/6.

points: Q-learning updates Q(s, a) += α [r + γ max_a' Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)]; it is off-policy, learning the greedy policy's values while behaving, e.g., ε-greedily.
With a tabular Q and enough exploration plus decaying step sizes, Q-learning converges to Q*, and the optimal policy is π(s) = argmax_a Q*(s, a).
Deep Q-networks approximate Q with a neural net, stabilized by experience replay and a slowly updated target network; the max operator also causes overestimation, which Double DQN reduces.

check.q: Why does DQN use a separate, slowly updated target network when computing r + γ max Q(s', a')?
choices: To stop the regression target from shifting with every gradient step
To allow the algorithm to learn on-policy from fresh data only
To convert the problem into a supervised task with true labels
To remove the need for exploration through ε-greedy actions
check.why: If the same rapidly changing network defines the target, training chases a moving target and can oscillate or diverge; freezing it periodically stabilizes learning. The targets are still bootstrapped, not true labels.

value_based_rl.tryIt: Implement tabular Q-learning on a 4x4 FrozenLake-style gridworld (deterministic) with ε-greedy exploration; print the greedy policy as arrows after 2000 episodes.

points: Policy gradient methods parameterize π_θ(a|s) and ascend J(θ) = E[Σ γ^t r_t] using ∇J = E[Σ_t ∇_θ log π_θ(a_t|s_t) G_t] (REINFORCE), which needs no dynamics model.
Subtracting a baseline b(s), such as V(s), from G_t leaves the gradient unbiased but lowers variance; using A(s, a) = Q(s, a) - V(s) gives the advantage form.
Actor-critic methods learn a critic (e.g. V_w via TD) to estimate advantages for the actor; PPO and similar methods also limit the policy change per update for stability.

check.q: In REINFORCE, you subtract a state-dependent baseline b(s) from the return. What does this change?
choices: It biases the gradient toward more conservative actions
It changes the optimal policy the method converges to
It removes the need to sample trajectories from the policy
It reduces gradient variance without introducing bias
check.why: E[∇ log π(a|s) b(s)] = 0 because the score function has zero mean, so the expected gradient is unchanged while variance drops. The objective and optimum are unaffected.

policy_gradient.tryIt: For a 2-action softmax policy on a bandit with rewards 1 and 0, estimate the gradient with 1000 samples with and without a baseline of 0.5, and compare the means and variances.

points: Model-based RL fits a dynamics model x_t+1 ≈ f_θ(x_t, u_t) from data, e.g. by least squares for linear systems (system identification) or with neural nets, then plans or controls with it.
It is typically far more sample-efficient than model-free RL, since each transition trains a reusable model; planning can use MPC, iLQR, or simulated rollouts.
Model errors get exploited by the planner, which seeks regions where the model is wrong; ensembles, uncertainty estimates, short horizons, and replanning with new data mitigate this.

check.q: A planner using a learned dynamics model finds a plan that looks great in the model but fails on the real robot. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The reward function was not differentiable with respect to actions
The discount factor was too small for the planning horizon
The planner exploited model errors in poorly covered states
Model-based methods cannot handle continuous action spaces
check.why: Optimizers push toward states where the learned model is inaccurate and overly optimistic; this model exploitation is the classic failure. Continuous actions are handled routinely, e.g. by MPC.

model_based_rl.tryIt: Simulate x_t+1 = A x_t + B u_t + noise for a 2-D system with random inputs, then recover A and B by least squares on stacked [x_t, u_t] and compare with the truth for 20 and 200 samples.

points: Behavior cloning treats imitation as supervised learning: fit π_θ(a | s) to expert pairs (s, a) by minimizing a loss such as squared error or negative log-likelihood.
It needs no reward and no environment interaction during training, making it simple and data-efficient when demonstrations cover the states the policy will visit.
Multimodal demonstrations (e.g. passing an obstacle left or right) break a unimodal regressor, which averages them; mixture models, diffusion policies, or action discretization help.

check.q: Half the demonstrations steer left around a pole and half steer right. A behavior cloning policy trained with mean squared error does what at the pole?
choices: Randomly picks left or right with equal probability each time
Averages the two and drives roughly straight into the pole
Refuses to act because the loss cannot be minimized
Always picks the side that appeared first in the dataset
check.why: MSE regression predicts the conditional mean, which for two symmetric modes is the middle, the worst choice. Sampling from modes requires a multimodal policy class, not plain MSE.

behavior_cloning.tryIt: Create a dataset where s is in [-1, 1] and the action is +1 or -1 at random; fit a linear regressor and a 2-component mixture (or classifier) and compare predictions at s = 0.

points: Training states come from the expert's distribution, but at test time the learner visits states induced by its own policy; small mistakes push it into states never seen in training.
Errors compound: with per-step error ε, behavior cloning's expected cost can grow like O(ε T²) over horizon T, versus O(ε T) when trained on the learner's own state distribution.
DAgger fixes this by rolling out the learner, having the expert label the visited states, aggregating the data, and retraining; noise injection during demos (DART) also broadens coverage.

check.q: A self-driving policy trained on perfect lane-centered human driving drifts off-center and then fails to recover. What fix addresses the root cause?
choices: Train longer on the same demonstrations to lower training error
Use a bigger network so it can memorize every expert state
Increase the discount factor so future errors are penalized
Collect expert labels on states the learned policy itself visits
check.why: The problem is that off-center states are missing from training; DAgger-style relabeling of the learner's own states supplies recovery data. Lower training error on expert states does not cover new states.

covariate_shift.tryIt: Simulate a 1-D lane-keeping task where the expert action is -k x; train a policy only on near-zero x, roll it out with small noise, and compare drift with a DAgger loop that adds expert-labeled visited states.

points: Inverse RL assumes the expert is near-optimal for an unknown reward R and seeks an R under which the expert's behavior beats alternatives, then solves RL for that R.
The problem is ill-posed: many rewards (including R = 0) explain the same behavior, so methods add structure such as feature matching or the maximum entropy principle.
A learned reward can transfer to new dynamics or environments better than a cloned policy, but IRL is expensive since it typically solves an RL problem inside its loop.

check.q: Why might inverse RL generalize better than behavior cloning when the robot is deployed in a new environment layout?
choices: The recovered reward captures goals, and replanning adapts to new dynamics
IRL does not need any demonstrations, so it avoids dataset bias
IRL produces a unique reward that is exactly the expert's true reward
IRL avoids solving any RL or planning problem during deployment
check.why: A reward encodes what the expert wants, so optimizing it in a new setting yields new appropriate behavior, while a cloned policy just maps states to actions seen before. IRL rewards are not unique, and it still needs demos and planning.

inverse_rl.tryIt: In a 1-D chain of 5 states, write two different reward functions (including a shaped one) that both make 'always move right' optimal, illustrating why IRL is ill-posed.
